evaluation.positioning_hook: At a supernatural office in New York, a witchy pizza run goes sideways when a demon crashes the night shift, forcing a snarky team of misfits to survive until sunrise.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is easy to grasp and the vampire-pizza-demon escalation gives it a clear genre promise, but the appeal is still fairly niche because the humor is very specific and the world is built around a small ensemble at one office. It has a real audience among horror-comedy and supernatural-fantasy buyers, but it is not an obvious four-quadrant play.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately: a supernatural office night shift turns into a contained monster problem, and the script keeps that engine legible from the first pizza run to the demon breach. The vampire pizza place, the ghost clients, and the demon summoning all reinforce one clean premise.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Joan, Cassandra, Mateo, and Willy each have a distinct comic function and enough friction to make the group fun to watch, especially in the apology beats and the final teamwork sequence. They are vivid enough to carry a feature, though the roles are more sharply defined by banter and function than by deep interior contradiction.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script has a fresh mash-up of office comedy, occult logistics, and creature chaos, with the Slack joke, the entity storage room, and the vampire pizza run giving it a playful identity. The voice is confident, though the underlying structure still sits in familiar 'misfits battle supernatural threat' territory.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story moves briskly from the pizza errand to the demon escalation, and each beat adds a new supernatural complication rather than stalling. The stakes are clear by the time the demon appears, though the first half spends a fair amount of time in banter before the central threat fully locks in.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The idea of a supernatural office that handles ghosts, witches, and demons is immediately ownable, and the pizza-run misfire is a clean, memorable trigger. It feels fresh in presentation even if the broad 'team survives a night from hell' shape is familiar.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The office has a usable internal logic: entity categories upstairs, talismans in drawers, Slack references, and a boss who clearly knows the supernatural bureaucracy. That texture makes the world feel story-generating, even though the script only sketches the larger rules rather than fully opening them up.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is sharply defined as profane, playful, and lightly grotesque, with the dialogue bouncing between workplace sniping and occult panic. The contrast between deadpan office rhythms and escalating monster imagery gives the script a distinct comic-horror flavor.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There are hints of a larger supernatural ecosystem and some interpersonal history, but the script mostly plays the surface-level comic engine rather than suggesting deeper thematic layers. The emotional material is functional and effective, but it does not yet imply a lot of hidden depth.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The ensemble is the engine: Joan and Cassandra’s rivalry, Mateo’s anxious loyalty, and Willy’s exhausted authority all generate scenes even before the demon arrives. The final stretch works because the group dynamics are already established enough that any pairing in the room has comic and dramatic charge.

lead_characters.name: Joan
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 20s-30s, witch/cosplayer-coded, New York-based, working-class or lower-middle-class vibe
lead_characters.hook: Joan is the sharp-tongued, easily provoked witch at the center of the chaos, the one who takes the vampire pizza run personally and turns embarrassment into action. She reads as defensive, proud, and more capable than she wants anyone to notice, with a chip on her shoulder about being underestimated by Cassandra and the office at large.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Aubrey Plaza in Ingrid Goes West — a prickly, funny, emotionally armored lead who can weaponize irritation and then pivot into real vulnerability. The role gives an actor a fast, quotable comic rhythm plus the payoff of being the person who actually has to perform the containment spell under pressure.

lead_characters.name: Cassandra
lead_characters.demographics: Woman, 20s-30s, witch, office insider, socially dominant
lead_characters.hook: Cassandra is the smug instigator with enough supernatural confidence to needle Joan and enough panic underneath to recognize when the room has gone wrong. She is the kind of character who can start trouble, apologize halfway through, and still feel like she owns the space.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Kathryn Hahn in Bad Moms — a high-energy, razor-tongued comic role that lets an actor be both the problem and the charm. It offers sharp banter, status play, and a late-scene turn into genuine team loyalty.

lead_characters.name: Mateo
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 20s-30s, anxious office runner, likely Latino-coded by name and vibe
lead_characters.hook: Mateo is the nervous heart of the office, a people-pleaser who keeps trying to do the right thing while getting dragged into supernatural nonsense he barely understands. His appeal is in the sincerity: he is awkward, loyal, and just brave enough to matter when the ghosts and demon show up.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Diego Luna in Narcos a chance to play intelligence under pressure, or that lets a comic actor like Michael Cera-style energy carry sincere panic. The showcase is the emotional pivot from anxious sidekick to the one who negotiates with the dead and helps hold the group together.

lead_characters.name: Willy
lead_characters.demographics: Man, 30s-50s, boss/occult operator, glasses, revolver, office authority
lead_characters.hook: Willy is the exhausted supernatural manager who seems half-asleep until the room turns lethal, then becomes the only person with a plan. He has the best authority energy in the script: dry, competent, and just weird enough to feel like he has been surviving this office for years.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of J.K. Simmons in Whiplash or Jeffrey Wright in Westworld — controlled authority with a dry edge and a sudden ability to dominate the room. The role gives an actor the pleasure of being the calm center, the lore keeper, and the guy with the bullet that matters.

lead_characters.name: Margaret
lead_characters.hook: Margaret is the old ghost who starts as a nuisance and becomes an ally, with a blunt, no-nonsense voice that cuts through Mateo’s panic. She gives the script a humanizing dead-world presence and a small emotional thread about unfinished business.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of late-breaking supporting turn that gave June Squibb in Nebraska or Margo Martindale in The Americans a chance to steal scenes with authority and specificity. The role is small but memorable, with comic bite and a sincere afterlife plea.

casting_characteristics: Ensemble of four core adults plus one featured ghost role
Performance needs strong comic timing and rapid dialogue handling

notable_requirements: Office/main hall, meeting room, lounge, back room, upstairs storage
One exterior pizza-place location and a brief street/alley beat
Contained practical locations with one hero supernatural office build

technical.vfx_details: Monsters, ghosts, floating runes, demon manifestation, and supernatural environmental effects like flickering lights and portal imagery; could be handled with selective practical augmentation and limited compositing.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical creature makeup/prosthetics, garlic-dust orb effect, talismans, bloodless demon effects, flicker and boom cues, and a few impact beats for chase movement.

rights_flags.detail: TikTok is named in dialogue as a threat.
Slack is referenced as the office communication system.

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: contained supernatural ensemble comedy-horror with streamer-friendly genre positioning.

budget.note: The script is mostly contained to a few office interiors, but the demon reveal, ghost effects, vampire restaurant, and chase sequence push it beyond a simple dialogue indie.

casting.note: The project needs four performers with fast comic timing and clean ensemble chemistry, plus a boss actor who can play deadpan authority without flattening the humor.

development.note: The premise is clear, the escalation is legible, and the supernatural office rules are easy to understand from the page.

audience_target.primary_audience: Viewers who like irreverent supernatural comedies with ensemble banter, practical creature chaos, and a strong midnight-movie vibe.
audience_target.demographics: Adults 18-44, slightly male-skewing but broadly balanced, with strongest pull among genre fans and comedy-horror audiences.

budget_tier.note: Mostly contained office interiors and one exterior pizza run, with moderate creature/VFX work and practical effects driving the spend.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of contained, character-forward genre films that can sell on tone, ensemble chemistry, and a memorable premise. The office setting keeps it producible while the demon/vampire/ghost material gives it enough spectacle for genre buyers.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature: the office ensemble is fun, but no supporting character is yet built as a clear spin-off anchor.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Supernatural office as a clean engine
strengths.what_it_means: This gives the project an instantly pitchable container that buyers can understand in one sentence and budget against without guesswork. It is especially attractive to streamer and indie genre buyers looking for a contained concept with repeatable comic rules.
strengths.evidence: The office has entity storage upstairs, talismans in drawers, Slack references, and a boss who already knows how to handle ghosts and demons.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Joan and Cassandra have real comic friction
strengths.what_it_means: The central relationship creates scene-level energy before the monster plot even kicks in, which is what makes the script feel castable and playable. That kind of banter-driven rivalry is exactly what attracts actor-forward buyers and directors who want ensemble chemistry.
strengths.evidence: The pizza-den argument, the cosplayer insult, and the apology beat all land because the two women have status tension and history.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Contained night structure with escalating threats
strengths.what_it_means: The one-night pressure cooker keeps the production footprint manageable while still delivering a full genre ride. Buyers looking for a contained feature with a clear start, middle, and monster payoff will understand the value immediately.
strengths.evidence: The story moves from pizza pickup to vampire chase to demon breach to sunrise aftermath without leaving the core location system for long.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The dialogue has a usable comic snap
strengths.what_it_means: The script has quotable, actor-friendly exchanges that can sell in a trailer and give performers room to make the material feel alive. That matters for casting because it signals a project where the cast can elevate the page without needing expensive spectacle.
strengths.evidence: Lines like 'Cool balls,' the Slack joke, and the office bickering around the pizza all show a fast, irreverent rhythm.

whats_special.headline: This is a contained, actor-friendly supernatural comedy-horror with a clear buyable engine: a weird office, a one-night monster problem, and a cast that can carry the joke-to-danger pivot. The production footprint stays in indie territory while the premise and tone are specific enough to stand out in the streamer-friendly genre lane.

items.area: The first act leans on banter before the threat locks in.
items.detail: The pizza-run setup and office teasing are fun, but the central monster engine does not fully seize the movie until the demon arrives late in the back half. That makes the opening feel more like a vibe and less like a hard narrative hook for a buyer skimming pages.

items.area: The supernatural rules are still sketchy.
items.detail: The office has talismans, ofuda, crucifixes, bullets, runes, ghosts, witches, and demons, but the script only partially explains how these systems relate. A producer would note that the world is fun, but the rule-set is still more suggestive than fully operational.

items.area: The ensemble is lively but still function-first.
items.detail: Joan, Cassandra, Mateo, and Willy all have distinct comic functions, but the page gives them more banter than interior contradiction. That keeps the movie playable, but it also means the cast conversation will center on chemistry rather than on a single role that feels like an awards-level showcase.

items.area: The creature work will need disciplined scope.
items.detail: The vampire restaurant, ghost manifestations, floating runes, and full demon reveal all ask for visible effects work in a short runtime. Even in an indie lane, that means the production has to stay disciplined about how much of the supernatural is shown versus implied.

issues.headline: The script’s main friction is that the opening plays as a comic hangout before the demon plot fully takes over, so the buyer conversation will focus on how quickly the premise truly lands. The world is appealing, but the rule-set and effects scope are still broad enough that the movie will need careful containment to stay inside its indie lane.
